subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How does PCl₅ react with the following? a) water b) C₂H₅OH c) CH₃COOH d) Ag

verification.note: Unit 7 (VA Group Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.83-84, from the shaded sub-box "VA GROUP ELEMENTS" of printed chapter 7 ("7. VA, VIA, VIIA GROUP ELEMENTS & NOBLE GASES"); the book prints this question and all four equations on book p.84 as the single Short Answer Question of this sub-box. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK CHECK (book p.84, SAQ 1): all four printed equations were atom-counted and all four are balanced. PCl₅ + H₂O (cold) → POCl₃ + 2HCl (P 1, Cl 5, H 2, O 1 each side); C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl (C 2, H 6, O 1, P 1, Cl 5 each side); CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl (C 2, H 4, O 2, P 1, Cl 5 each side); PCl₅ + 2Ag → 2AgCl + PCl₃ (P 1, Cl 5, Ag 2 each side). They are reproduced unchanged. BOOK GAP: the book writes "(cold)" beside the water equation but never gives the reaction with EXCESS water, which is the other half of that part and gives H₃PO₄. It is added here (PCl₅ + 4H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 5HCl, atom-counted: P 1, Cl 5, H 8, O 4 each side). TREND: the card also records why PCl₅ exists at all while NCl₅ does not — phosphorus has vacant 3d orbitals and can expand its octet, nitrogen has no d orbitals in its valence shell and cannot.

steps.label: With water
lines: a) With a little cold water PCl₅ gives
With excess water the hydrolysis is complete
steps.why: The amount of water changes the product, so the condition has to be written beside the equation. A little cold water replaces two chlorine atoms and stops at POCl₃; excess water replaces all five and gives H₃PO₄.
common_mistakes: Writing H₃PO₄ for the cold, limited water case. That product needs excess water.
Leaving out the word cold or limited. Without it the first equation looks wrong beside the second.
steps.memory_tip: Little water stops at POCl₃; plenty of water goes all the way to H₃PO₄.
steps.margin_note: Write both cases with their conditions. The examiner is checking that the condition is understood, not only the formula.

steps.label: With ethanol
lines: b) The –OH group of the alcohol is replaced
This is a standard laboratory method for
making an alkyl chloride from an alcohol.
steps.why: PCl₅ replaces one –OH group per molecule and is left as POCl₃ plus one HCl. That is the difference from PCl₃, which converts three –OH groups and is left as H₃PO₃, and it is why the coefficients here are all 1.
common_mistakes: Writing H₃PO₃ or H₃PO₄ as the phosphorus product. With an alcohol, PCl₅ gives POCl₃ and HCl.
Using a coefficient of 3 as in the PCl₃ reaction. One PCl₅ converts one alcohol molecule.
steps.memory_tip: PCl₅ with an –OH always leaves POCl₃ and one HCl behind.
steps.margin_note: All three products must be written. The HCl is the one most often left out.

steps.label: With acetic acid
lines: c) The –OH group of the carboxylic acid is
This is how acid chlorides are prepared
steps.why: A carboxylic acid contains an –OH group just as an alcohol does, so it reacts in exactly the same pattern and gives the same two phosphorus-containing products. Writing parts (b) and (c) with the same shape shows the examiner that the pattern was recognised.
common_mistakes: Writing CH₃COCl with two oxygens. The –OH has gone, so acetyl chloride has one oxygen.
Naming the product acetic chloride. Its name is acetyl chloride, or ethanoyl chloride.
steps.memory_tip: Alcohol gives an alkyl chloride; carboxylic acid gives an acyl chloride. Same reagent, same pattern.
steps.margin_note: One balanced equation earns this mark. Naming the product is a useful extra line, not a required one.

steps.label: With silver
lines: d) With finely divided silver on warming,
PCl₅ acts as a chlorinating agent:
Two of the five chlorine atoms go to the
silver, so PCl₅ is reduced to PCl₃ and the
steps.why: This part is a redox reaction and not a substitution: phosphorus falls from +5 to +3 while silver rises from 0 to +1, and two silver atoms are needed for the two electrons. Naming which species is oxidised and which reduced is what separates this part from the first three.
common_mistakes: Writing AgCl₅ or Ag₂Cl. Silver is +1, so the chloride is AgCl and two of them are formed.
Leaving PCl₃ out of the products. The phosphorus does not disappear; it is reduced to PCl₃.
steps.memory_tip: Silver takes two chlorines, so PCl₅ drops to PCl₃. Five minus two is three.
steps.margin_note: The balanced equation is the mark. Adding the words oxidised and reduced makes the answer complete.

insider_note: Part (a) with a little cold water, and parts (b) and (c), all leave POCl₃ behind; with excess water part (a) goes all the way to H₃PO₄. Part (d) is the only redox one — that grouping is the fastest way to keep the four equations straight. It is also worth knowing that PCl₅ exists because phosphorus has vacant 3d orbitals, while NCl₅ does not exist because nitrogen has no d orbitals in its valence shell.
